newsitem.title: UK: FEATURE-Dlr to stay king of commodities after EMU.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-Dlr to stay king of commodities after EMU.

text.p: The planned single European currency promises to transform many world markets, but commodities traders and analysts say their key contracts will continue to be dominated by the dollar.

Few envisage a euro challenge to the dollar as the currency in which items like gold, grains, oil or base metals are valued in worldwide trade, not least because Europe's role in commodity markets is shrinking.

"Europe's declining role in commodity markets and the strength of emerging consumers in the Far East are far more important raw materials trends than the Euro," said Hans-Joachim Timm at Hamburg's HWWA economic research institute.
EURO IMPACT TO BE SLIGHT
Commodity traders wait to be surprised, but at the moment they think the impact of European Economic and Monetary Union (EMU) on their business will be slight.
It may make it easier to calculate the subsidies that European taxpayers hand out to their farmers, and a handful of futures contracts may need to be tinkered with.
But any long-term economic impact so far as it may affect raw material demand is seen as too hypothetical to discuss now.
Clive Furness, a director at the London International Financial Futures and Options Exchange (LIFFE), believes EMU is not an issue for commodity markets.

A merger this month saw LIFFE subsume the oldest European tropical commodity market, the London Commodity Exchange. One reason was to rescue it from likely U.S. takeover and another was to try to promote a European sector in the Chicago-dominated trade in grains futures.
GRAIN TO STAY IN DOLLAR DOMAIN

A new LIFFE wheat contract would look like a prime candidate for being denominated in the euro. But top brokers don't rule out that this, too, could end up using the dollar. Banks would find it easier to offer foreign exchange cover against a dollar contract closer to its Chicago counterpart and to realities of the $40 billion physical trade in world grain.
"Grain will always be first and foremost an American market," said a senior EU farm official.
HWWA's Timm said that, as competitors to sell grain like the U.S., Australia and Latin America all used the dollar, the EU would have to quote in it "if it wants to keep its markets."

Trade in wheat further depends on a matrix of prices for other cereals like corn (maize) in which the EU is less active. Nearly half world corn is grown in the United States. Trading in gold will see "no impact arising from the introduction of European Monetary Union given that the market is so dollar driven", added Allan Baker, chairman of the London Bullion Market Association. Among soft commodities, traders in cocoa also saw scant impact beyond possibly switching a London futures contract from sterling to the Euro.

"Maybe if everyone in Europe is buying physical cocoa in euros it will make things a little simpler but the effect will be negligible," said Paul Naar, managing director at Gerkens Cacao in Amsterdam which is part of U.S. trader Cargill.
CURRENCY RISK INSIGNIFICANT

EMU will limit currency risk on trading within Europe and mean less hedging. But this is not seen as too significant. "We're a guilder company with a dollar-based parent so we already hedge currencies. Hedging possibilities these days are so sophisticated anyway that there won't be much effect," said Naar at Gerkens Cacao.

Fundamentals have meanwhile tended to outweigh speculation against currency swings in grains trading within Europe lately. "There is a lot of supply and demand in these markets. For example Spain had a big deficit last year so they imported a lot from Britain," said Steve Thornhill, head of marketing at Britain's Home Grown Cereals Authority.

The hub of world trade in the industrial metals led by copper and aluminium is the London Metal Exchange. Chief executive David King said his board had considered the EMU issue but had not issued any formal guidance yet as the situation seemed unclear.

Copper, aluminium, zinc and nickel are listed as far out as 27 months. This means that from the beginning of October, January 1999 -- the scheduled launch date for EMU -- will fall into the LME price structure.
The flagship contracts are all in dollars but the LME also lists others in yen, marks and sterling, fixed daily basis a midsession currency conversion rate.
Open interest in these is very low. Latest LME data for copper shows a total 188,919 contracts but only 561 are listed in sterling and marks.
"Not too many people are talking about (a Euro contract) at this stage because it is so far ahead. But I know that some customers in Europe do want it," a metals trader said.

Monetary union may make life easier for EU bureaucrats who calculate how much taxpayers' cash they pay in internal subsidies, and for the farmers who collect those handouts. They are already set in a notional single currency, the Ecu, but at special "green" rates of exchange that have to be established against individual member state currencies.

It involves a complex formula that a single currency would in theory abolish. But measures like green rates would be needed as long as some states did not join it, said Joachim Heine, European Commission director of Agro-Economic legislation. -- London Newsroom (44 171 542 7729) with contributions by commodity reporters in Amsterdam, Brussels, Hamburg and Paris
